reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A leading cause of irreversible central visual loss in older adults, affecting fine detail, reading, and face recognition while peripheral vision is spared
Dry (non-exudative) form is commonest and progresses slowly with drusen and retinal pigment epithelial changes, culminating in geographic atrophy
Wet (neovascular/exudative) form is less common but causes rapid, severe loss due to choroidal neovascularisation, haemorrhage, and fluid
New distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) or a central blur/scotoma, often monitored with an Amsler grid, suggests conversion to wet AMD and warrants urgent referral
Smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor; age, family history, and pale iris/light exposure also contribute
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection is the mainstay for neovascular AMD and can stabilise or improve vision
Dietary antioxidant and zinc supplementation can reduce progression risk in intermediate dry AMD
reference.pathophysiology: Age-related macular degeneration results from cumulative damage to the retinal pigment epithelium, Bruch's membrane, and choriocapillaris at the macula. Impaired clearance of metabolic debris leads to drusen deposition, and oxidative stress, complement-mediated inflammation, and lipofuscin accumulation injure the photoreceptor-RPE complex. In the atrophic form this causes progressive loss of central photoreceptors, whereas in the neovascular form ischaemia and VEGF release drive abnormal choroidal new vessels that leak and bleed beneath and within the retina, rapidly destroying central vision.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination and colour fundus photography
Optical coherence tomography to detect intraretinal/subretinal fluid and atrophy
OCT angiography or fluorescein angiography to identify choroidal neovascularisation
Amsler grid for self-monitoring of distortion
Visual acuity and near vision testing
redFlags: Sudden central distortion, blurring, or a new scotoma suggesting conversion to neovascular AMD — urgent referral
Sudden severe drop in central vision from submacular haemorrhage
Rapid progression in the second eye of a patient with unilateral wet AMD
Any acute change while on anti-VEGF therapy indicating recurrent activity
reference.prognosis: Dry AMD progresses slowly and central vision may remain functional for years, whereas untreated wet AMD can cause rapid severe central loss; prompt anti-VEGF therapy substantially improves outcomes, though peripheral vision is preserved in all forms.
pitfalls: Dismissing new metamorphopsia as needing new glasses and delaying urgent referral for wet AMD
Failing to advise smoking cessation as a key modifiable risk
Assuming peripheral vision loss is due to AMD, when it points elsewhere
Not checking and monitoring the fellow eye, which is at high risk
management: Treat neovascular (wet) disease with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections such as ranibizumab, aflibercept or bevacizumab on a regular or treat-and-extend regimen
Offer antioxidant and zinc supplementation of an AREDS-type formulation to slow progression in intermediate or advanced dry disease
Strongly advise smoking cessation as the most important modifiable risk factor, and address diet and cardiovascular risk
Arrange Amsler grid self-monitoring with urgent re-referral for new distortion or central scotoma signalling conversion to wet disease
Monitor with optical coherence tomography to guide retreatment and detect recurrent fluid
Provide low-vision rehabilitation, magnifiers and registration as sight-impaired for those with established central loss
Refer promptly to ophthalmology, urgently when neovascular conversion is suspected
